content: The Chilean Pharmaceutical Policy was an initiative introduced during the 1960s and 1970s to establish a rational national pharmaceutical policy. Chile is considered to be the first country in the world to implement the concept of a limited list of essential drugs. In 1965, under the administration of President Eduardo Frei, measures were taken to rationalize the supply and use of pharmaceuticals. By 1967, a national formulary containing a restricted list of drugs was established. In 1970, Dr. Salvador Allende was elected president, and efforts to rationalize the pharmaceutical supply system continued. The next phase of this policy involved organizing centralized bulk procurement of pharmaceuticals. In 1971, the first international tender for raw pharmaceutical materials was announced. However, this move was met with resistance from the pharmaceutical industry. Within three months of the tender announcement, widely used medications, including analgesics and antibiotics, disappeared from the market as manufacturers deliberately reduced production. The pharmaceutical companies agreed to restore the supply of these drugs within a week only if the international tenders were canceled. In 1972, the government was compelled to abandon the tender process due to the pressure exerted by the pharmaceutical industry. By 1973, the government of Salvador Allende was overthrown, and the pioneering essential drug program that had been initiated came to an end.
